title: What does the affected filesystem show?
summary: Start with read-only capacity and inode checks on the filesystem used by the failing application.
why: Byte exhaustion and inode exhaustion produce similar application symptoms but require different investigation.

commands.purpose: Show filesystem block usage in human-readable units.

choices.label: The output is unclear or unavailable

title: Does directory usage explain the filesystem usage?
summary: Compare directory totals without crossing into other filesystems.
why: A large difference between filesystem usage and visible files can indicate deleted-but-open files, reserved blocks, snapshots, or hidden mounts.

commands.purpose: Compare top-level directory usage on one filesystem. Results may be incomplete when permissions prevent traversal.

choices.label: A directory tree explains the growth
Visible files are much smaller than df usage

title: Inode exhaustion is likely
summary: Many small files can exhaust inodes while substantial byte capacity remains.
why: Creating new files requires free inodes as well as free blocks.

commands.purpose: Locate directories with unusually many entries; review scope before running on very large filesystems. Results may be incomplete without sufficient permissions.

title: Are you checking the same mount the application writes to?
summary: Confirm the application path and its backing filesystem.
why: Bind mounts, container layers, temporary filesystems, and separate data volumes can make the wrong filesystem appear healthy.

commands.purpose: Show the filesystem backing the actual application path.

choices.label: The path maps to another full filesystem

title: Are deleted files still held open?
summary: A process can retain disk blocks after a pathname is deleted.
why: Space is released only after the last open file descriptor is closed.

commands.purpose: List open files whose link count is below one. Sufficient privileges may be required to see files held by other users or services.

choices.label: A process holds a large deleted file

title: What type of data is growing?
summary: Identify ownership, retention policy, and service impact before cleanup.
why: Size alone does not determine whether data can be safely removed.

title: Review a scoped cleanup or retention fix
summary: Use the owning service’s retention, rotation, pruning, or archival mechanism rather than deleting unfamiliar files blindly.
why: Direct deletion can break recovery, audit, database, or service assumptions.
rollback: Restore from backup or reverse the service-specific retention change where possible.

choices.label: A reviewed cleanup or retention change was completed
The change is not clearly safe

title: Review whether the owning process can be safely restarted
summary: Closing the final file descriptor releases deleted-file space, but restarting a production process may cause service impact.
why: The process, not the deleted pathname, currently owns the allocated blocks.
prerequisites: Identify the process and service owner.
Confirm restart procedure and expected impact.
rollback: Use the service rollback/failover procedure if the restart causes degradation.

choices.label: The process safely released the file
Restart is unsafe or ownership is unclear

title: Verify capacity and service recovery
summary: Confirm the original symptom is resolved and capacity remains stable.

commands.purpose: Confirm both block and inode availability.

verification: Free blocks or inodes increased as expected.
The affected application can create or write files again.
Filesystem growth is stable during an observation period.

choices.label: Capacity and service behavior are healthy

title: Recovery verified
summary: Record the growth source, retention gap, monitoring gap, and prevention action.
prevention: Alert on both block and inode consumption.
Review log/data retention and container cleanup policies.
Monitor growth rate, not only static thresholds.

title: Escalate with preserved evidence
summary: Do not delete data blindly. Share filesystem, mount, inode, directory-usage, and open-file evidence with the system or application owner.
